work: The Elder or Poetic Edda, trans. Olive Bray (Viking Club, 1908)
label: Collingwood

pictures.title: Óðinn in Torment
pictures.caption: This scene is from prose prologue to the poem Grimnismál in the Viking Society's reprint of Olive Bray's dual language edition of The Elder Edda (1908). W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts the moment when Agnarr, the son of King Geirröðr, takes pity on the mysterious guest that his father is torturing.

pictures.title: Fulla on Her Way to Geirröðr's Court
pictures.caption: This scene is from prose prologue to the poem Grimnismál in the Viking Society's reprint of Olive Bray's dual language edition of The Elder Edda (1908). W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts Frigg's servant Fulla, and an unnamed companion, on their way to King Geirröðr's court. Frigg has sent Fulla with a message warning the King that a dangerous enchanter is coming in disguise to his kingdom.

pictures.title: Alvíss Answers Þórr
pictures.caption: This scene is from prose prologue to the poem Alvissmál in the Viking Society's reprint of 's dual language edition of The Elder Edda (1908). W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts Þórr confronting a dwarf named Alvíss who wants to marry his daughter Þruðr.

pictures.title: Alvíss Turned to Stone
pictures.caption: This scene is from prose prologue to the poem Alvissmál in the Viking Society's reprint of 's dual language edition of The Elder Edda (1908). W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts a dwarf named Alviss who has just been turned into stone by the first light of day. Alviss engaged in a wisdom contest with Þrúðr´s father Þórr who outwitted him by prolonging the contest until daylight. 110 90 Wood Engraving

pictures.title: Víðarr Slaying Fenrir
pictures.caption: This scene is from prose prologue to the poem Vafþrúnismál in the Viking Society's reprint of 's dual language edition of The Elder Edda (1908). W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts Víðarr slaying Fenrir by holding his jaws apart and stabbing him after the wolf has killed Óðinn at the Battle of Ragnarök.

pictures.title: Óðinn's Last Words to Baldr
pictures.caption: This scene is from prose prologue to the poem Vafþrúnismál in the Viking Society's reprint of Olive Bray's dual language edition of The Elder Edda (1908). W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts Óðinn whispering into the ear of his deceased son Baldr, who is laying on his funeral pyre.

pictures.title: The Stranger at the Door
pictures.caption: This scene is from prose prologue to the poem Hávamál in the Viking Society's reprint of Olive Bray's dual language edition of The Elder Edda (1908). W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts a traveller knocking on a door.

pictures.title: Odin's Self-sacrifice
pictures.caption: This scene is from prose prologue to the poem Hávamál in the Viking Society's reprint of Olive Bray's dual language edition of The Elder Edda (1908). W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts Óðinn sacrificing himself to himself, by hanging from a tree for nine nights and being pierced with a spear, in order to gain the knowledge of runes.

pictures.title: Þórr Slays the Ox
pictures.caption: This scene is from prose prologue to the poem Hymiskiða in the Viking Society's reprint of Olive Bray's dual language edition of The Elder Edda (1908). W. G. Collingwood's depicts Þórr twisting the head off of an ox in order to use it for bait on a fishing trip with the giant Hymir.

pictures.title: Þórr's Fishing Trip
pictures.caption: This scene is from prose prologue to the poem Hymiskiða in the Viking Society's reprint of Olive Bray's dual language edition of The Elder Edda (1908). W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts Þórr reeling Miðgarðsormr in to the side of the boat.

pictures.title: Loki's Flight to Jötunheimr
pictures.caption: This illustration by W.G. Collingwood is from Olive Bray's translation of the Poetic Edda that was published in a dual language edition in 1908 as The Elder or Poetic Edda: Commonly Known As Sæmund's Edda. The illustration depicts Loki flying in Freyja´s feather cloak to Jötunheimr in order to discover the whereabouts of Þórr´s missing hammer.

pictures.title: Þrymr's Wedding-feast
pictures.caption: This illustration by W.G. Collingwood is from Olive Bray's translation of the Poetic Edda that was published in a dual language edition in 1908 as The Elder or Poetic Edda: Commonly Known As Sæmund's Edda. The illustration depicts the giant Þrymr trying to kiss his bride, who is actually Þórr disguised as Freyja, at their wedding feast. Þrymr has stuck a deal with the gods that he will return Þórr´s hammer in exchange for being allowed to marry Freyja.

pictures.title: The Lovesickness of Freyr
pictures.caption: This illustration by W.G. Collingwood is from the poem Skirnismál in Olive Bray's translation of the Poetic Edda that was published in a dual language edition in 1908 as The Elder or Poetic Edda: Commonly Known As Sæmund's Edda. The illustration depicts a lovesick Freyr pining for the giantess Gerðr whom he has glimpsed from afar. The couple in the background are his parents Njörðr and Skaði who are concerned about the source of their son´s unhappiness.

pictures.title: Skirnir's Message to Gerðr
pictures.caption: This scene is from the poem Skirnismál in the Viking Society's reprint of Olive Bray's dual language edition of The Elder Edda (1908) published under the name as The Elder or Poetic Edda: Commonly Known As Sæmund's Edda.. W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts Freyr´s servant Skirnir wooing the giantess Gerðr on Freyr´s behalf.

pictures.title: Gróa's Incantation
pictures.caption: This scene is from the poem Gróagaldr in the Viking Society's reprint of Olive Bray's dual language edition of The Elder Edda (1908). W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts Svipdagr listening to a deceased seeres, i.e., his mother Gróa, telling him charms that will protect him when he goes to woo Menglöð.

pictures.title: Svipdagr finds Menglöð
pictures.caption: This scene is from the poem Gróagaldr in the Viking Society's reprint of Olive Bray's dual language edition of The Elder Edda (1908). W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts Svipdagr embracing Menglöð.

pictures.title: Þórr Threatens Hárbarðr
pictures.caption: This scene is from the poem Hárbarðsljóð in the Viking Society's reprint of Olive Bray's dual language edition of The Elder Edda (1908). W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts Þórr brandishing his hammer and exchanging insults with a ferryman named Hárbarðr who is refusing to ferry Þórr brandishing across a river.

pictures.title: Hárbarðr Mocks Þórr
pictures.caption: This scene is from the poem Hárbarðsljóð in the Viking Society's reprint of Olive Bray's dual language edition of The Elder Edda (1908). W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts Þórr exchanging insults with a ferryman named Hárbarðr who is refusing to ferry Þórr across a river. Hárbarðr is one of the many names that Óðinn uses and the details in the poem suggest that the ferryman is Óðinn in disguise.

pictures.title: Rígr in Great-grandfather's Cottage
pictures.caption: This illustration by W.G. Collingwood is from Olive Bray's translation of the Poetic Edda that was published in a dual language edition in 1908 as The Elder or Poetic Edda: Commonly Known As Sæmund's Edda. This scene is from the poem Rígsþula and depicts a traveller named Rígr, who is actually Heimdallr in disguise, sitting with a childless couple who will become the parents of a son named Þrall after Rígr stays with them.

pictures.title: The Crow Warns Kon
pictures.caption: This illustration by W.G. Collingwood is from Olive Bray's translation of the Poetic Edda that was published in a dual language edition in 1908 as The Elder or Poetic Edda: Commonly Known As Sæmund's Edda. This scene is from the poem Rígsþula and depicts a boy was born after Rígr visited his parents. Kon, who is known as "Kon ungr'"understands the speech of birds and is destined to become a king someday, i.e., konungr." The bird in the illustration is telling Kon that it is time for him to set aside childish pursuits and become a warrior.

pictures.title: Heimdallr and His Nine Mothers
pictures.caption: This illustration by W.G. Collingwood is from Olive Bray's translation of the Poetic Edda that was published in a dual language edition in 1908 as The Elder or Poetic Edda: Commonly Known As Sæmund's Edda. This scene is from the poem Völuspá En Skamma in the Viking Society's reprint of Olive Bray's dual language edition of The Elder Edda (1908). W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts "Heimdal and his Nine Mothers."

pictures.title: The Vision of the Mighty One
pictures.caption: This illustration by W.G. Collingwood is from Olive Bray's translation of the Poetic Edda that was published in a dual language edition in 1908 as The Elder or Poetic Edda: Commonly Known As Sæmund's Edda. This scene is from the poem Völuspá En Skamma in the Viking Society's reprint of Olive Bray's dual language edition of The Elder Edda (1908). W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts the last verse: There shall come hereafter --> another mightier whose name I dare not --> now make known: few there are --> who may see beyond when Odin fares --> to fight with the Wolf. (v. 17 223)

pictures.title: Freyja Awakes Hyndla
pictures.caption: This illustration by W.G. Collingwood is from Olive Bray's translation of the Poetic Edda that was published in a dual language edition in 1908 as The Elder or Poetic Edda: Commonly Known As Sæmund's Edda. This scene is from the poem Hyndluljóð in the Viking Society's reprint of Olive Bray's dual language edition of The Elder Edda (1908). W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts Freyja waking the giantess Hyndla. Freyja askes Hyndla to ride to Vallhöll with her, but she does not tell Hyndla that the boar with her is actually Óttarr who is seeking information concerning his ancestry.

pictures.title: The Ancestry of Óttarr
pictures.caption: This illustration by W.G. Collingwood is from Olive Bray's translation of the Poetic Edda that was published in a dual language edition in 1908 as The Elder or Poetic Edda: Commonly Known As Sæmund's Edda. This scene is from the poem Hyndluljóð in the Viking Society's reprint of Olive Bray's dual language edition of The Elder Edda (1908). W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts Óttarr and his kin, along with Hyndla´s words from the last line of verse 29, "allt´s þat ætt þín, Óttarr heimski!" (All this race is thine, Ottarr the Simple!"

pictures.title: Hermóðr's Ride to Hel
pictures.caption: This illustration by W.G. Collingwood is from Olive Bray's translation of the Poetic Edda that was published in a dual language edition in 1908 as The Elder or Poetic Edda: Commonly Known As Sæmund's Edda. This scene is from the poem Baldrs Draumar. W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts Óðinn riding Sleipnir on his way to consult a seeress regarding Baldr´s disturbing dreams.

pictures.title: The Death of Baldr
pictures.caption: This illustration by W.G. Collingwood is from Olive Bray's translation of the Poetic Edda that was published in a dual language edition in 1908 as The Elder or Poetic Edda: Commonly Known As Sæmund's Edda. This scene is from the poem Baldrs Draumar. W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts Loki who is about to guide Hoðr´s arm to throw a spear made of mistletoe at Baldr.

pictures.title: Loki taunts Bragi
pictures.caption: This illustration by W.G. Collingwood is from Olive Bray's translation of the Poetic Edda that was published in a dual language edition in 1908 as The Elder or Poetic Edda: Commonly Known As Sæmund's Edda. This scene is from the poem Lokasenna. W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts Loki insulting Braggi and his wife Iðunn at Ægir´s feast.

pictures.title: Loki Bound
pictures.caption: This illustration by W.G. Collingwood is from Olive Bray's translation of the Poetic Edda that was published in a dual language edition in 1908 as The Elder or Poetic Edda: Commonly Known As Sæmund's Edda. This scene is from the poem Lokasenna. W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts Loki in torment after the gods have bound him with the guts of his son Narfi. Skaði has placed a snake over Loki´s head to drip venom on him and his wife, Sigyn, is trying to catch the venom.

pictures.title: The Battle of Ragnarök
pictures.caption: This illustration by W.G. Collingwood is from Olive Bray's translation of the Poetic Edda that was published in a dual language edition in 1908 as The Elder or Poetic Edda: Commonly Known As Sæmund's Edda. W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts the Battle of Ragnarök. Collingwood placed his illustration within the framework of the Haysham Hogback.

pictures.title: After the Battle of Ragnarök
pictures.caption: This illustration by W.G. Collingwood is from Olive Bray's translation of the Poetic Edda that was published in a dual language edition in 1908 as The Elder or Poetic Edda: Commonly Known As Sæmund's Edda. This scene is from the poem Völuspá. W. G. Collingwood's illustration depicts the restoration of the world after the Battle of Ragnarök and the Mighty Ruler whose coming is prophesied in verse 65. Collingwood placed his illustration within the framework of the Haysham Hogback.
